title: Chapter 13 – What the Vulture Keeps
html:
[Blood Shadow Sect – Gu Yan]

The eye will not stop weeping.

Gu Yan lies on a shelf of black rock in the back of a cave, in the dark, with a strip of wet cloth over the left side of his face, and he listens to the ice sing. The Frostfang ridge is forty miles northeast of Green Pine Hill, high enough that the springs freeze in their beds by midwinter and the wind comes down off the glacier with a sound like a long knife being drawn from a sheath. He chose the cave for the cold. Cold slows blood. Cold slows pain.

Neither is slowing now.

He lifts the cloth and presses two fingers against the ruined socket, and the fire starts again, a thin bright wire running from the corner of the eye straight back into the center of his skull. He breathes through it. He has been breathing through it for two days.

It is only pepper. He keeps telling himself that. Pepper, and some kind of oil, and a talisman of the cheapest grade sold in any market in four valleys, thrown by a boy of fourteen with a leg he could not stand on. In forty-one years of walking the Blood Path, Gu Yan has been cut by Profound blades, scorched by Yellow-grade fire arrays and once, memorably, half-drowned by a woman at the late stage of Foundation Establishment who had a good deal of rage in her. None of it hurt like this. A burn he can feed on. A wound he can drink down and turn into more of himself. But the pepper is not Qi and it is not flesh. It is simply a thing that lives in the eye and screams, and there is nothing in the Blood Shadow canons that tells him how to eat it.

He sits up, slowly, the way he does everything now, and reaches for the bowl.

It sits on a flat stone beside his shelf: a wide shallow dish of black glass, rimmed with silver, half full of water the color of rust. He picks up the knife beside it, the small one, and opens his left palm along an old scar, and lets nine drops fall into the water.

The water shivers. A thin red thread unwinds from the center and crawls toward the rim.

"Not yet," he tells it, and closes his hand around the cut.

Not yet. First he needs to think. And to think, he needs to remember, in order, exactly how a hunt he planned for twenty days came apart in the space of a hundred breaths.

\ \ \*

It had been a very good plan.

That is what bothers him most. Gu Yan is not a fool. He does not take contracts without reading the ground, and he spent six days reading the Salt Hollow before the Lins' hunters arrived: the trail, the springs, the charcoal burners' hut, the one narrow gap in the rocks on the north side that is the only way out. He lay on a ledge above the hollow in the cold for two nights, with the Crimson Vulture Cloak pulled over him and his breath held to a thread, while the deer came down to the salt and nothing came after them. He had never had a better ambush.

His buyer had given him the day. The hour. The names.

That was the part he had liked least, and had accepted anyway. The buyer was a man named Zhao Bei, a stout, sweating steward from Red Ridge who arrived at Gu Yan's camp on a mule, with a purse of three hundred low-grade stones and a manner that said he would rather be anywhere else. Zhao Bei did not explain who had told him the Lins' plans, and Gu Yan did not ask. A man who sells his own family for a gambling debt is common enough. What mattered was the price.

Make the Lin hill bleed, Zhao Bei had said, reciting. Their juniors, their guards, their hunters. Not the Patriarch, not his heir. Nothing that will bring the Sect's wardens to the door. Let them think it is demonic vermin passing through.

Demonic vermin. Gu Yan had smiled at that, a little. It is not an insult if it is accurate.

So he waited, on the ledge, with Sha across his knees. The blade does not like waiting. It is a short, curved, ugly thing the length of a forearm, forged from the thighbone of some beast Gu Yan's master never named and quenched, over forty years, in the blood of everything it has cut. Profound grade, his master said, though Gu Yan has never seen another Profound weapon that hungers the way it does. When it is quiet, it hums, very faintly, in a register just below hearing. When it smells blood it starts to sing.

It sang loudly, on the second morning, when the Lins came down the trail.

Four of them. An old limping man with a short sword and the settled walk of a veteran, and he was strong, a solid sixth layer of Qi Refining with earth Qi that pressed on the air like a hand on a drum. A boy with a spear, tall, sharp-faced, perhaps fourteen. Two younger cousins. One of them, a round-cheeked boy, had the green gleam of a healing art in his hands and the bright, quick, unguarded Qi of the very young.

Gu Yan had planned to take them in order: the old man last, the boy with the spear second to last, and the cousins first. The cousins to feed, the others to frighten. A body drained in front of its friends is worth ten bodies merely killed.

He took the round-cheeked boy first. It was quick. A step out of the mist, two fingers to the throat, the Draw, a long pull on the blood and the Qi riding in it, and the boy went white and folded up like a bird. He tasted spring grass, he tasted warm bread, he tasted a mother's voice calling someone in from the yard. The usual. Young blood is sweet in the way of unripe fruit.

And then he had turned to the boy with the spear, and had almost forgotten the rest of the hunt.

Gu Yan has seen perhaps six thousand people in his life and drunk from several hundred. He has an eye for roots. He knew, as soon as the mist cleared, what he was looking at, the way a jeweler knows a stone in a pile of gravel: three elements, wood, fire and earth, all of them clean, none of them dominant. A triple-root spiritual body in a child of fourteen who had never been to a master or eaten a single pill. The blood of a boy like that does not simply feed. It builds.

He had smiled. He remembers smiling. He remembers thinking: The Sect will give me anything for you.

Then the earth wall had gone up between them, and the stone shards had come off the floor of the hollow in a hail, and he had walked through both of them with his mantle lit and his mist thickening, because a man at the third layer of Foundation Establishment does not stop for a sixth-layer earth wall. He remembers the old man's face, set and white, the cane thrown aside, the short sword rising. He remembers deciding to kill him last.

And the boy, the tall, bleeding, terrified boy with the three roots, had pulled a bit of orange paper out of his jacket and thrown it directly at Gu Yan's face.

It was not a clever throw. It was not a skilled one. It was a boy throwing a scrap of paper at a man's eyes from eight feet away, with his arm shaking. Gu Yan had not even bothered to block it. A Flame-Burst, he thought. A first-rank fire talisman. He had been burned by such things as a child and would not feel it through the mantle.

The talisman burst a hand's breadth from his face. And the world went white and red and unbearable.

He does not remember the next ten breaths. He remembers the screaming, and that it was his. He remembers that the mist had gone out of his control because the Qi that held it had been scattered by pain; that his left eye felt as though someone had driven a red-hot nail into it and then poured acid after; that he could not see out of the right one either, for the tears. He remembers the second talisman hitting the ground at his feet and bursting, and the smoke going up his nose and into his throat. He remembers going down on one knee, retching, with the Crimson Vulture Cloak smoking around him, and thinking, with a clarity he could not explain: this was made for me.

Not for an animal. Not for a bandit. For a thing that fights with its senses. Someone had thought about what a cultivator with a blood-sense does when something burns his face, and had built an answer out of paper and pepper and a child's good aim.

\ \ \*

When his sight cleared enough to stand, they had gone.

He followed the blood. Of course he followed the blood. The old man was carrying the boy, running, Gu Yan could hear them in the rocks, and the thorn thicket on the hollow's north rim was thick, and in forty yards he would have caught them. He had Sha out and singing. He had the Draw halfway to a boil in his chest. He cleared the thorns and saw the old man, with the boy over his shoulder and one wounded leg, scrambling toward the lip of the hollow and the long slope down.

And he saw the hollow's rim light up from behind.

Not fire. Cold. A white mist poured down over the stones, and where it touched, the thorn bushes went rigid, hissed, and frosted solid. Something struck him in the chest, hard, a bolt of water hurled so fast and so dense that it had the weight of an iron rod. It went through the mantle like an awl through wet paper and shattered two ribs on the way. He was thrown backward ten feet and landed in the salt.

He had looked up through his tears, and she was standing there at the lip of the hollow in a gray hunting jacket, a slim, small woman with a knife at her back and her hand still extended, blue light dying on her fingers.

The Tidal Spear, he thought. That is the Stream-Ghost line. That is an old rogue art. The last teacher of that style was a woman named

He did not finish the thought. A second bolt had been coming, and he rolled, and then the iron rod came out of the dark.

An old man. Gaunt. One-armed. The wrapped right sleeve pinned across his chest, a long rod of black iron in his left hand, a leather case under his arm. A man who walked with a heavy slouch and moved like a snake. The rod caught Gu Yan's wrist, and the bone cracked, and Sha went out of his hand and rang off a rock.

Gu Yan looked up into the old man's face.

He knew it. That was what he could not get past, lying in the salt with his ribs broken and his one good eye streaming. He knew that face. Fifteen years older and thinner, the beard gone gray, the left eye, once a hard black, now clouded at the edges. But he had seen it a hundred times on a wall in the Hall of the Veiled Forge, a portrait with a name written under it in dark red.

Hu Tieshou. The Smith of Coral Gate. Deserter.

The old man had looked down at him without recognition, without hate, with the flat attention of a craftsman examining a flaw in a casting, and drawn back the rod for the stroke that would crush his skull.

And then a voice, from the rim of the hollow, calm and old, said: "Hu. Leave him. The boys are bleeding."

Gu Yan had turned his head.

The Patriarch of the Lin family stood at the top of the slope with a long notched sword in his hand, and the air around him was wrong. It shimmered. The snow on the ground beneath his feet had melted in a ring ten feet wide. And the air coming off him, thin, smothered, and held in so tightly that it was almost not there, was the smell of an oven.

An old man at the ninth layer of Qi Refining. He had known that. Everyone knew that.

But the old man's Qi was not that of a man at the end of his road. It was banked. Compressed. The Qi of a fire that has been starved for decades and has just been told that it will not have to go out. And Gu Yan, who had stood in front of more than one Foundation Establishment cultivator and lived, understood in a single cold breath that the old man had a card in his sleeve that no one in four valleys knew about. One he would play if he had to. Once.

Zhao Bei did not know, he thought. Zhao does not know.

It was enough. He did not need to know what it was. He rolled, and put every drop of Qi he had left into the Mist Step, and went down the slope in a cloud of red haze, snatching Sha off the rock as he went, leaving the Vulture Cloak's tail feathers behind and his ribs grinding and his eye on fire. Behind him, the old man had not even moved. He had simply stood there with his sword in his hand, and let him run.

That was what Gu Yan could not forgive. They had let him go.

\ \ \*

Before he calls the Elder, he does what every Blood Shadow cultivator learns to do after a bad fight, and takes inventory.

The ribs first: two cracked, one broken, the lung nicked but not pierced. He has set them with a binding of red thread and a poultice of grave-moss and heart-root, and eaten one of the Elder's pills, a Grade 3 Marrow Knitting Pill, bitter as old copper. The wrist is worse. The old man's rod has shattered the small bone below the thumb and the bone is going to take a month, and there is nothing for it but time and blood.

The cloak next. He lays it across his knees, the Crimson Vulture Cloak, Yellow grade, forty years old, cut from the feathers of a red-crowned vulture that his master hunted down in the Corpse Desert and wore, and then wore out, and then gave to his best pupil. It has served him well. The mantle woven into the feathers turns aside blades of the Yellow grade and below. Tonight there are three burn holes the size of coins in the left shoulder and the tail is gone. It will not turn another Tidal Spear.

And Sha. He lays the blade on the stone beside the bowl, and it hums, softly, hungrily, in the register below hearing. It has not fed in two days. It knows it has not fed. He lays the flat of his good hand against the bone-white edge, the way one calms a dog, and tells it what he tells it every night: soon.

There is a nick in the edge near the guard, from where it rang off the rock. A tiny one. He frowns at it. In forty years it has never been nicked. A blood blade quenched in so many lives should heal itself by morning.

He runs his thumb along the nick, and does not know why it troubles him.

\ \ \*

The water in the bowl has turned the color of dark wine. He bends over it.

A face forms on the surface: lean and gray, with sunken eyes and a mouth like a seam in leather. It does not look at all like the face of a man who has been sleeping.

"You are alive," says Elder Mu. "I had been told you were not."

"Told by whom, Elder?"

"Zhao's steward sent word that the Lins had a guest elder with an iron rod." The thin mouth does not move much. "And that a cultivator in a feather cloak had fled the hollow. I was inclined to wait and see whether you would have the grace to die of it."

The Elder is a man at the middle stage of what the Blood Shadow Sect calls the Pool, which the rest of the world calls Foundation Establishment. The Sect has its own ladder for everything, and Gu Yan has spent forty-one years climbing it. The Drip, Qi Refining, where the body learns to swallow Qi from outside. The Pool, where a cultivator builds a lake of blood and Qi inside himself that does not drain. The Well, which the Sect says is the Purple Mansion, and the Rill, which the Sect says is a Golden Core and which no one now living has seen. Ranks, that is, the Elder's face on the water reminds him, that Gu Yan is a long way from.

"I have found him," says Gu Yan.

"Who?"

"Hu Tieshou. The Smith of Coral Gate."

Silence. The thin face stills.

"Say that again."

"He is teaching in the Lin house. He is an artificer there. I saw him with my own eyes, Elder. One-armed. A rod of black iron. The right sleeve pinned. And he moves like a man who has not lost a single step." Gu Yan swallows. His ribs grind. "He put my wrist through in a single stroke."

For a long time, the Elder says nothing at all. The water ripples as if something has dropped into it from a great height.

"Fifteen years," he says finally, very softly. "We burned the whole of Coral Gate looking for him. We took his arm. We were certain he was dead."

"Not dead."

"No." There is something in the voice that Gu Yan has never heard in it before, and it takes him a moment to understand that it is fear. "Not dead. Hiding among farmers in the Tianyuan Realm, with a great deal of our blood still in his body. And he took with him the Hundred Veins Forge Canon. All nine volumes. I will tell you that the Sect has been waiting fifteen years for that book."

"What do I do?"

"You do nothing," the Elder says. "Do you understand? Nothing. Do not touch the old man. Do not touch the house. You are a Pool at the third stage with one eye. You will be dead in ten breaths. I will send others."

"The boy," says Gu Yan, quietly.

The face looks at him through the water.

"There was a boy at the hollow. Fourteen, perhaps. Triple root. Wood, fire and earth, all of them clean. Elder, I tasted it in the air."

"Triple-root," the Elder repeats.

"A boy like that would fill the Well-Hall's blood-urn for a year. And he was there. He threw the talisman. He is in the Lin house. With Hu." Gu Yan's one good eye is steady. "If you send others, send me with them. I owe that house an eye."

Another long silence. The Elder is thinking. Gu Yan watches the thin mouth work.

"Twenty days," the Elder says at last. "Heal. Eat the three-stage pills I have left in your cache. I will find out what is happening in the Eastern Sea and who knows what about the Smith, and I will decide who comes. You will be told. Until then, you are not to go within ten miles of that hill."

"And the Zhao?"

The face on the water smiles for the first time. It is not a pleasant sight.

"The Zhao want the Lins ruined without a witness. We want the Smith, and the book, and a boy with three roots. For twenty days, let the Zhao believe we are their dogs." The water goes still. "Dogs, after all, can be told where to bite."

The connection breaks. The red thread dissolves into the water, and the face is gone.

Gu Yan sits back against the cold rock and breathes.

\ \ \*

He does not sleep.

Instead he lies on the black shelf in the dark and does what he has done on many other nights when a plan has failed: he sorts what he knows.

The Lin house has a Patriarch at the ninth layer who has something in reserve. That is one fact. The old man did not strike him down when he could have, when Hu's rod was already raised. That is another fact, and an odd one. A man with a card like that does not hold back because he is merciful. He holds back because he is afraid of what a kill would draw.

Zhao is not the only one with reasons to keep the Sect's wardens away.

There is a woman in that house who throws water like an iron bar and fights in the Stream-Ghost style, which means that the Patriarch's daughter-in-law is a rogue, and a good one. That is a third fact. There is the Smith, who has been hiding for fifteen years and has finally been found. A fourth.

And there is the pepper.

The more he thinks about it the less he likes it. Zhao Bei's people told him the Lins have three hunters of any note and a farm full of guards, and none of them have ever thought about a blood cultivator's eyes. It is not an obvious weakness. It is not written in any manual. It is the sort of thing a man learns by fighting a blood cultivator and surviving, or by studying one, patiently, with a good deal of curiosity, from a distance. The Smith could have thought of it. But a Smith of the Veiled Forge does not make talismans.

He reaches into the torn lining of the cloak and brings out what he picked up in the hollow, a scrap of paper the size of a thumbnail, singed brown at one edge and still stinking of pepper. A fragment of the second talisman.

He holds it up in the faint blue light that leaks in from the cave mouth.

The paper is wrong. He sees it at once. It is too fine and too even, with no cloud in it and no seam, so smooth that light passes through it like light through silk. He has handled talisman paper in every market from the Coral Gate to the Beast Mountains, and he has never touched anything like it. The ink is the same: a clean orange-red, the strokes sharp-edged and uniform, the lines of the circuit so true that even in a scrap he can follow the loop.

The Smith did not make this. The Smith makes iron.

Someone in that house has found a way to make paper, and ink, and talismans, that no one in four valleys can match. And that same someone sat down with that paper and thought about what a blood-drinker does when his face is on fire.

The same hand. Or two hands who talk to each other.

He thinks, for no reason he can name, of the sixth-layer earth cultivator with his short sword and cane, who had put up a wall to protect a boy, and of the boy, who had not aimed at the chest or the sword arm or the heart, but at the eyes. Somebody had told him to. Somebody had given him exactly three slips of paper, and exactly one instruction.

It is nothing. A scrap of paper, and a feeling.

But he is a man who has lived forty-one years on the Blood Path by remembering the small things, and he folds the scrap very carefully into a pouch at his belt, and cuts open his palm a second time and lets a single drop fall onto the stone beside the bowl, and says a name into the dark in a voice that is almost gentle.

"Lin Wenhai."

There is no answer. There will not be one for some days. But he knows, as surely as he knows his own pulse, that a man who sells his family for a debt can be bought again, for a different price, and a different debt. Zhao Heng's steward has not been told that the hunter in the feather cloak keeps his own accounts.

Twenty days. An eye to heal. A book to find, a boy with three roots, and somebody in that house who knows how to make paper that sees.

Outside, the wind off the glacier rises. The ice sings. And in the dark, on the black shelf, the vulture closes his one good eye and begins, patiently, to count.
